Name: set_completion_retrieval
Title: Knowing the Set but Not the Members: Mechanisms of Incomplete Set-Valued Knowledge Retrieval in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM must retrieve a SET of answers (e.g., 'list all countries that border France', 'name the members of a band'), it internally represents the full set's membership in a distributed 'set signature' but fails to serialize it completely during generation: members compete for the next-token slot, already-emitted members suppress remaining ones, and the model prematurely commits to a stop. We hypothesize that (1) the set's true cardinality and unemitted members are partially decodable from internal activations even when the model stops early or omits them, (2) omissions are predictable from an inhibition dynamic in which emitted-member directions suppress the retrieval directions of remaining members, and (3) a lightweight 'emitted-member suppression removal' intervention recovers dropped members without hallucination.
Related Work: Single-fact recall circuits (Geva et al. 2023; Fierro et al. 2024) and factual localization (Hochman et al. 2026) study one subject-attribute answer, never set enumeration. Multi-hop latent reasoning work (Yang et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2025) composes facts within a pass but does not address set/list retrieval. Retrieval-gap and interference proposals (my prior work) concern single-target retrieval and fact-fact collisions, not the sequential dynamics of enumerating a known set. Applied work (Itharajula et al. 2026; plant-science list queries) documents behaviorally that LLMs return incomplete, unreliable lists and recommends GraphRAG as a workaround, but offers no mechanistic account of WHY parametric list retrieval is incomplete. No prior work localizes an internal set-membership representation, characterizes emitted-member inhibition during serialization, or provides a mechanistic intervention to recover dropped members. This is the first mechanistic study of set-valued knowledge retrieval and its serialization bottleneck.
Abstract: Language models are notoriously unreliable when asked to enumerate a set—listing all countries bordering France, all members of a band, all elements in a group—returning incomplete lists, dropping obvious members, and stopping early. It is unknown whether these failures reflect missing knowledge or a failure to serialize knowledge the model actually holds. We propose that LLMs represent set membership as a distributed 'set signature' in intermediate activations but struggle to convert it into a complete generated list because of a serialization bottleneck: candidate members compete for each next-token slot, already-emitted members inhibit the retrieval of remaining ones, and the model commits to termination before the set is exhausted. We test three claims. First, we probe whether the full set's membership and cardinality are linearly decodable from the residual stream at the query position, even for members the model ultimately omits (knows-the-set-but-drops-members). Second, we characterize the inhibition dynamic: during generation we track the retrieval direction of each true member and test whether emitting a member causally suppresses the residual-stream activation of the remaining members via attention to already-generated tokens. Third, we introduce two training-free interventions—(a) suppression-removal, which projects out the aggregate emitted-member direction before predicting the next member, and (b) a set-cardinality-aware stop calibration derived from the decoded cardinality signal—and measure recovery of dropped members (recall gain), hallucination rate (must not fabricate non-members), and stop accuracy. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3 across scales on curated finite-set queries with verifiable ground-truth membership.
Experiments: 1) BENCHMARK: Curate ~2k finite-set queries with fully verifiable ground-truth membership and known cardinality, spanning (a) geographic sets (countries bordering X; US states in a region), (b) compositional/relational sets (movies directed by X; children of X), (c) categorical/definitional sets (planets; noble gases). Restrict primary analysis to sets whose members are INDIVIDUALLY retrievable (verified via single-member membership probes: model correctly answers 'Does Y border France?' or completes the fact) so failures are enumeration, not knowledge, failures. 2) SET-SIGNATURE PROBE: At the query position (before/at list onset), train linear probes on residual-stream activations per layer to decode (i) membership of each candidate (member vs non-member classification over a candidate pool) and (ii) set cardinality (regression). Report probe AUROC/accuracy, especially for members the model later OMITS, to test 'knows-but-drops'. 3) OMISSION CHARACTERIZATION: For each generated list, classify errors as omissions (true member missing), hallucinations (non-member emitted), duplicates, and early-stop. Report rates by set type and cardinality; test whether omission probability rises with position/list length. 4) INHIBITION DYNAMIC: During generation, track the next-token logit and residual-stream retrieval direction for each not-yet-emitted true member across steps. Test the hypothesis that emitting member m reduces the retrieval-direction strength of remaining members. Causally validate with attention-knockout: ablate attention from the current position to already-generated member tokens and measure whether suppressed members' logits recover. 5) INTERVENTIONS: (a) SUPPRESSION-REMOVAL: at each list step, estimate the aggregate emitted-member direction (difference-of-means of already-generated member representations) and project it out of the answer-position residual before predicting the next member; measure recall gain and hallucination rate. (b) CARDINALITY-AWARE STOP: use the decoded cardinality to set a target list length and discourage EOS until reached; measure stop accuracy and recall/precision. Baselines: no intervention, temperature/beam variation, explicit 'list exactly N' prompting, self-consistency, and random-direction projection control. 6) SCALING/GENERALIZATION: Repeat on Pythia (1.4B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B); test whether set-signature decodability improves and omission rates shrink with scale, and whether the suppression direction transfers across set types. METRICS: set-membership probe AUROC (incl. on omitted members), cardinality decoding error, omission/hallucination/duplicate/early-stop rates, inhibition effect size, attention-knockout recovery, intervention recall gain, hallucination delta, F1, stop accuracy, scaling trends.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Probe decodability of omitted members may overstate 'knowing'; we require causal corroboration (attention-knockout recovery, intervention effects) and treat decodability as necessary-not-sufficient. 2) Some sets have ambiguous/temporally-shifting membership; we use only well-defined finite sets with stable ground truth. 3) Individual-member retrievability verification is imperfect (a model may recognize but not recall a member); we report on both recognition and recall variants. 4) Suppression-removal risks reintroducing duplicates or emitting non-members; hallucination and duplicate rates are explicit success criteria. 5) Cardinality-aware stopping could over-extend lists into hallucination when the decoded cardinality is wrong; we measure precision alongside recall and report cardinality-decoding error. 6) Effects may be architecture/scale specific (GQA vs MHA); we characterize across families rather than assume universality. 7) Enumeration may partly reflect general in-context copying/counting limits rather than knowledge retrieval; we disentangle by comparing knowledge-set enumeration against a matched in-context list-copying control task.
